title: In Praise of Audiobooks
author: Jenna A. Robinson
summary: Jenna A. Robinson argues that audiobooks are one of the best ways to hook children on good fiction before they can decode it themselves. She starts from the decline in fiction reading, citing the National Endowment for the Arts and Gallup, and from research linking fiction to empathy. Her key point is that listening comprehension develops faster than phonetic decoding, so children who can barely read simple texts can already follow far richer stories. Audiobooks bridge that gap and help when parents lack time to read long books aloud. She cites fMRI research showing that reading and listening engage similar brain regions, while conceding that nonfiction and textbooks may be better read on paper. She closes with a practical invitation to try full-cast and well-narrated audiobooks with children and tie the habit to a more empathetic civic life.
points: Listening comprehension outpaces decoding, so audiobooks give young children access to stories they cannot yet read themselves.
Fiction, whether read or heard, builds empathy, a capacity the author says a divided culture badly needs.
Reading and listening activate similar brain regions, supporting audiobooks as a legitimate way to take in fiction.
Audiobooks suit fiction best, while nonfiction and textbooks may still be better read on paper.
quotes: Because listening comprehension develops faster than phonetic decoding skills, children who can barely read “See Spot Run” may already understand Little House in the Big Woods.
Audiobooks bridge the gap, opening up more interesting works that children can understand but cannot yet decode on their own.
Humans listen before they read. During development, the brain doesn’t build a dedicated reading pathway. It uses the speech system already in place and asks it to improvise.
Studies using functional MRI show that reading and listening to audiobooks activate similar regions of the brain.
While nonfiction and textbooks may be better read on paper, audiobooks are excellent for fiction.
Listening to great works of fiction gives us practice in seeing others as flawed human beings who deserve dignity, rather than as enemies to be destroyed.
